lesson.title: Which One's Driving? Identifying the Explanatory Variable
lesson.summary: The explanatory variable is the one you use to predict or account for changes in another variable, a role determined by the question being asked, not by the data itself.
lesson.body:
A variable, as you already know, is any characteristic that can differ from one individual to the next: age, test score, phone brand, hours of sleep. When you study the relationship between two variables, though, it becomes useful to assign each one a role. The explanatory variable is the one you use to explain, predict, or account for differences in the other; it is the input side of the relationship, the variable whose value you already know or can control. This idea extends the two-way table and association work you just finished, except now the explanatory and response roles get names of their own and the tools you will eventually use, scatterplots and correlation, are built for quantitative rather than categorical data.

Which variable counts as explanatory is not a fixed property of the variable itself; it depends entirely on the question a particular study is asking. Hours of sleep might be the explanatory variable in a study predicting next-day test performance, but the same hours-of-sleep variable could be the response in a different study examining whether caffeine intake explains how much someone sleeps. By convention, whenever you build a scatterplot to examine a relationship, the explanatory variable goes on the horizontal x-axis, which is the same axis convention you already use for the categories along the bottom of a segmented bar graph.

Consider a small study relating hours spent studying to exam score: five students studied for 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 hours, and scored 60, 68, 75, 82, and 90 respectively. Here, hours studied is the explanatory variable, since the researcher is using study time to explain or predict the resulting score; it is the variable a student could actually choose to change before the exam. The average of the explanatory values is (1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4 plus 5) divided by 5, which equals 3 hours, giving a natural reference point for describing whether a given student studied more or less than typical.

Labeling hours studied as explanatory does not, by itself, prove that studying causes higher scores. It only tells you which variable is playing the role of predictor in this particular analysis. A rise in score alongside a rise in study hours is consistent with a causal effect, but it is equally consistent with a confounding variable, such as general motivation, driving both study time and exam performance upward together. The explanatory label describes the structure of the analysis, not a guarantee about cause and effect.

Every explanatory variable needs a partner: the outcome it is being used to predict or account for. That partner has its own name and its own role in the relationship, the response variable, which is the subject of the next section and which, together with the explanatory variable, completes the vocabulary you need to describe any two-variable relationship precisely.
